ECON 8310: Business Forecasting (with AI)

University of Nebraska at Omaha · Department of Economics

Forecasting tools and applications for business settings. The first half of the course covers traditional econometric forecasting; the second half turns to predictive analytics and machine learning. Everything is implemented in Python.

Course documents

About this course — what it teaches, what it assumes you already know, and the books it reads from.

Enrolled at UNO? Canvas has what this site does not

This site carries the course materials — every slide deck, lab, assignment, the book and the workbook — and nothing specific to one university, term or section. It has no calendar dates, no grading scale, no lecture recordings and no course policies.

If you are enrolled, Canvas is authoritative for all of those: your syllabus, the term calendar and due dates, the lecture videos, the academic-integrity and accessibility policies, and how work is submitted and graded. Where the two ever disagree, Canvas wins.

Textbooks

All are free online. None needs to be purchased.

BookUsed for
FPP-Py — Forecasting: Principles and Practice, the Pythonic Way Lectures 1–3; the primary text
FPP3 — the R edition Same material, R code. Chapter 12 is numbered differently — both numbers are always given
ISLP — An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python Lectures 4–6. FPP covers no tree methods and no regularization; this fills that gap
BMCP — Bayesian Modeling and Computation in Python Lectures 10–12. PyMC and ArviZ throughout, which is what we use

Before the first lab

Every lab and homework in this course reads from prepared data files that are not in the repository. Run these three commands once, from the repository root, before Week 1:

python scripts/prep_m5.py            # M5 / Walmart — the course spine
python scripts/prep_fred.py          # FRED macro series — Lecture 2
python scripts/prep_electricity.py   # hourly electricity demand — Lecture 3

Each downloads from a public source, needs no login or API key, and writes to data/processed/. Once they have run, nothing in this course needs the network again.

macOS users: one extra step before Week 5

XGBoost will not import on macOS without the OpenMP runtime. Install it once with brew install libomp, then pip install xgboost. Do this before Lab 5 rather than during it.

New to Quarto? Start here

Setup and Quarto guide — installing Python, Quarto and an editor (VS Code or Positron), what a .qmd file is, and the four errors you will hit. Google Colab will not work — it cannot open .qmd files.

When something breaks later — a package that will not install, a render that fails, a lab that errors halfway — go to Troubleshooting first. It covers the failures this course actually produces.

You will also need: jupyter, pandas, numpy, matplotlib, statsmodels, scikit-learn, prophet, pygam, xgboost, torch, pymc, and arviz. jupyter is not optional — Quarto runs your Python through a Jupyter kernel. Assignment submission, the AI workflow, and the prompt log live in the course environment repository.

Each assignment has a prompt budget

Every assignment carries a prompt budget and an initial context prompt that does not count against it. Any AI assistant is fine — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot — in an editor or a browser tab. UNO's ChatGPT Edu workspace does not include Codex, so nothing here requires it. You submit a PROMPT_LOG.md alongside your rendered work, listing every prompt you sent in order.

The budget is a target, not a limit. It exists to make you decide what is worth asking, and you may go over it — log the extra prompts and say where you got stuck. What does cost you is a log that does not match the work you submit.

The course as a book

Every lecture, in one continuous document you can read, search and quote from — the slides and what was said about them, assembled into fifteen numbered chapters. Useful for revision, for reading ahead, and for finding the lecture where a method was introduced without opening five decks.

Read the book →

The labs and assignments as a workbook

The companion volume: all fourteen labs and eleven assignments in one searchable document. Code is shown rather than run, so it opens instantly — each lab links to its executable version for when you are actually working. Every step carries a collapsible walkthrough of what was said about it in class, and every lab ends with the output your own run should produce.

Open the workbook →

It is generated, not written separately

The book is assembled from the decks themselves, so a table, figure or number in it cannot disagree with the lecture it came from. If a deck is corrected, the book carries the correction the next time it is built.
